analysis.one_liner: Repeals the rule requiring prevailing local wages on federally funded highway and transit construction.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended prevailing-wage protections for construction workers on federal-aid highway and transit projects, got no cosponsors, never received a hearing, and died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires that laborers and mechanics building federally funded highways and public transit projects be paid at least the locally prevailing wage — the rate common for that kind of work in that area. This bill would have deleted that requirement, letting contractors pay whatever wage they chose on those projects. It also applied to transit projects. The bill was introduced by Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC) on July 23, 2019, was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Education and Labor Committees, and never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors and firms bidding on federal-aid highway and transit projects. With no wage floor, they could lower their labor costs on taxpayer-funded work, widening margins or making bids cheaper.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 113 of title 23, U.S. Code, which requires laborers and mechanics on federal-aid highway projects to be paid no less than the locally prevailing wage rate.
Repeals Section 5333(a) of title 49, U.S. Code, which imposes the same prevailing-wage requirement on public transportation projects.
The repeal would take effect 31 days after enactment, but would not apply to contracts already in existence or made under bids outstanding on the date of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded highway and transit projects, who could see their pay cut to whatever wage a contractor offers, since the local prevailing-wage floor would be gone.
analysis.who_pays_short: Construction workers on federally funded projects

drawbacks.text: Workers on these projects could be paid less than the going local rate for their trade, because the bill repeals the prevailing-wage requirement for both federal-aid highway projects and public transportation projects.

The cost of the wage floor falls on contractors, not just workers' paychecks: an honest supporter would argue that prevailing-wage rules raise the cost of federally funded construction, so repeal could stretch Highway Trust Fund dollars across more projects or lower bids. The bill's title itself frames the repeal as 'Highway Trust Fund Reform.'

The counter-argument supporters of wage floors make: prevailing-wage standards are intended to keep government-funded projects from bidding down local construction wages, and removing the floor shifts the benefit of public spending toward contractors rather than the workers doing the work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs almost entirely to contractors, in the form of lower labor costs on federally funded projects, while the cost falls directly on the workers who build the projects. Whether repeal would meaningfully stretch federal transportation dollars is a contested question in wage-policy debates, but the bill contained no offsetting protections for workers and no mechanism ensuring savings were passed to taxpayers. It never received enough support even for a committee hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, then sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC) introduced the bill in the House on July 23, 2019.

The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and Labor, with consideration split between them to be determined later by the Speaker.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, where it remained; no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded highway and transit projects kept prevailing-wage protections, because the bill died without a cosponsor, hearing, or vote. Contractors who would have benefited from paying market-set wages gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on July 23, 2019.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; Chair held no hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on and no committee or floor vote was ever held, so the record shows only that a single Republican sponsored the bill and no member — of either party — moved it forward.

industries.note: The bill would have removed the prevailing-wage floor on federally funded projects, letting contractors cut labor costs on taxpayer-funded work. The saving flows to the firms' margins while the wage cut falls on the workers.

Workers on federal-aid highway and transit projects would lose the guarantee of the locally prevailing wage, which is the standard that keeps government projects from bidding down area construction pay. Their interest here runs with the public's interest in wage standards on public works.
